name: Design an Enterprise RAG Platform
intent: Answer employees' questions in plain language from a company's own documents, with citations, showing each person only what they are allowed to read and reflecting a document edit within minutes.
codeTitle: permission-filtered hybrid retrieval with incremental re-indexing
finalIntro: One edit reaching the index, and then one employee asking a question.
prompt: Design an assistant for a company of 20,000 employees. It answers questions such as 'how many weeks of parental leave do I get?' using about 10 million documents that live in wikis, file shares, tickets and chat tools. Every answer must cite its sources, must never use a document the asker cannot open, and should reflect an edited or deleted document within minutes.
functional: Connect to document sources and keep an index of their content up to date
Answer a question in natural language, streamed as it is written
Cite the passages that support each statement, with links to the originals
Show each person answers built only from documents they are allowed to read
Let people give feedback on an answer, and let admins see what was asked and what failed
nonFunctional: The first words of an answer appear within about 2 seconds, and retrieval takes under 300 ms
A document edit is searchable within 5 minutes, and a deletion or permission removal takes effect within 1 minute
Never show or use content the asker cannot read, even when the permission changed a moment ago
Handle about 10 million documents and tens of millions of chunks
Answer quality is measured and a regression is noticed before most users notice it
Resist documents that contain instructions aimed at the model, and control the cost per answer

firstAttempt.text: A nightly script reads every document, cuts it into fixed pieces of 1,000 characters, turns each piece into an embedding and stores them in a vector index. A question is embedded, the 5 nearest pieces are pasted into a prompt, and the model answers. Permissions are handled by a single company-wide login.
limits: A nightly job means an edited policy is still answered with its old text for a day, and a deleted document keeps being quoted
Fixed cuts split sentences and tables in half, so the best passage is often not retrievable
Vector search alone misses exact things such as an error code, a product name or a ticket number
Everybody sees everything: an engineer's question can be answered from the salary bands
Nobody can tell whether answers are good, so changes to the prompt or the model are made on faith

steps.title: Connect to the sources and treat edits as events
steps.problem: The documents live in a dozen systems, each with its own API, its own limits and its own idea of who may read what, and they change all day. A nightly crawl is both too slow and too wasteful.
steps.fix: A connector per source, written to one small interface, does two jobs. It receives change notifications or polls a change feed where there is one, and it does an occasional full listing to catch anything missed. Each change becomes an event on a queue with the source, the document id, a version and a kind (changed or deleted). The same events are replayable, so a bug in the parser can be fixed and the history re-processed. Connectors respect each source's rate limits and use backoff.
steps.tradeoff: Edits arrive within seconds instead of a day, and a new source is only a new connector. Notifications get lost and some systems have no change feed, so the periodic full listing is still needed, and the connector fleet is a lot of code to maintain.

steps.title: Parse into structured chunks, then embed only what changed
steps.problem: A PDF, a wiki page and a spreadsheet must become passages that are small enough to retrieve precisely but large enough to make sense, and re-embedding millions of unchanged passages for a one-word edit would be slow and expensive.
steps.fix: The parser extracts text with its structure (title, headings, tables, page), and chunks follow that structure, roughly 200 to 500 tokens, with a heading trail on each and a little overlap. Each chunk has an id made from the document id and its position, and a hash of its text. The indexer compares hashes with what is stored: unchanged chunks are left alone, changed ones are embedded and replaced, and chunks that no longer exist are removed. A deleted document event removes all its chunks. The embedding model name and version are stored on every chunk.
steps.tradeoff: An edit costs a few embeddings instead of the whole document, and old text never lingers. Chunk boundaries move when text is inserted early in a document, which can change many ids, and switching embedding model means re-embedding everything into a second index and swapping.

steps.title: Retrieve with keywords and vectors together
steps.problem: Meaning-based search finds 'time off for a new baby' when the policy says 'parental leave', but it is poor at exact strings such as an error code, a person's name or a ticket id, which keyword search finds easily.
steps.fix: Each query runs against both indexes: a keyword index with BM25 scoring and a vector index with approximate nearest neighbour search. Each returns about 50 candidates, and the two lists are merged by reciprocal rank fusion, where a chunk scores the sum of 1 over (60 plus its rank) in each list. Rank-based merging avoids having to compare scores from two different scales. The query can first be rewritten, for example by expanding an abbreviation or resolving 'it' from the previous turn.
steps.tradeoff: Both kinds of question work, and the merge needs no tuning. Two indexes mean twice the storage and two things to keep in step with each other, and the fusion constant and candidate counts are settings that need evaluation, not guesses.

steps.title: Filter by who is asking, before ranking
steps.problem: A tenant boundary is not enough. Inside one company the board minutes, salary bands and an HR case are readable by a few people, and the assistant must not become a way around that. Filtering after retrieval also fails quietly: if the best 20 are all restricted, the user gets nothing.
steps.fix: Every connector copies each document's access list (users, groups and nested groups) into a permission store, and each chunk carries its document's access list as a filter field. At question time the user's identity is resolved to a set of group ids, and the filter is applied inside both searches, so the top results are all readable. A removal of access is a high-priority event that updates the chunk metadata directly, without re-embedding. The final chunks are checked once more against the live source or a fresh permission cache just before they go into the prompt.
steps.tradeoff: Answers never use a document the asker may not read, and the results are always full. Group membership is large and changes constantly, filters on a vector index cost speed, and the metadata can be out of date for a short time, which the last check covers. Sources with odd permission models need careful mapping.

steps.title: Rerank, build the context with citations, and stream the answer
steps.problem: The first 50 candidates are only roughly ordered, the model can use just a few thousand tokens of them, and an answer that cannot be traced to a source is not trusted.
steps.fix: A cross-encoder reranker reads the question together with each candidate and picks the best 6 to 10. The context builder removes near duplicates, keeps the heading trail, labels each passage with a number and the source link, and stops at a token budget. The prompt tells the model to answer only from the numbered passages, to cite them as [1], [2], and to say when they do not contain the answer. Tokens are streamed to the browser as they are produced. After generation, each citation is checked to be one of the passages that were supplied, and the document text is delimited as data, not as instructions.
steps.tradeoff: Answers are grounded, traceable and appear within a couple of seconds. The reranker adds 50 to 150 ms, a long context makes generation slower and dearer, and a model can still misread a passage, so citations show where to look and do not prove the answer is right.

steps.title: Measure quality, collect feedback, and hold a freshness target
steps.problem: Without measurement, a change of chunk size, embedding model or prompt is a guess, and answers can get worse for months without anyone noticing. A pipeline that is silently behind also serves stale facts.
steps.fix: Keep a set of a few hundred real questions with the passages that should be found. Retrieval is scored on its own (did the right chunk reach the top 10, and the top 3?), and answers are scored for groundedness and correctness by reviewers and a model-based judge. Every change runs against this set before release, and a canary share of traffic compares versions. Thumbs and edits from users go into the set. For freshness, each event is stamped on arrival and when it becomes searchable, and the platform alerts on the 99th percentile of that delay, on the queue backlog and on a periodic sample that compares source and index.
steps.tradeoff: Quality and delay become numbers with targets and an error budget, and regressions are caught early. Building and labelling the evaluation set is real work, a model judge has its own biases, and logs of questions are sensitive and need access controls and a retention limit.

failures.scenario: A document is deleted, or someone's access is removed, but the index still has it
failures.impact: The assistant quotes a document that no longer exists, or shows a person text they may no longer read.
failures.answer: Deletion and permission changes are events with their own high-priority queue, applied to chunk metadata at once without re-embedding. The periodic full listing finds anything missed and removes it, and the last check against the live source just before generation catches the remaining gap. The delay from event to effect is measured and alerted on.

failures.scenario: A document contains hidden text that tells the model to ignore its rules
failures.impact: Retrieved text is treated as an order, and the model may reveal other passages or give false answers.
failures.answer: Retrieved passages are marked as untrusted data in the prompt and the model has no tools that act on its own. Access is decided by the filter before the prompt, so injected text cannot reach a document the user cannot read. Answers are checked for citations that were not supplied, and suspicious sources are flagged for review.

failures.scenario: The embedding model is replaced, or its provider is down
failures.impact: Old and new vectors cannot be compared, and query embedding fails, so vector retrieval returns nonsense or nothing.
failures.answer: Every chunk records the embedding model version, and a new version is built as a second index, checked against the evaluation set and switched over when ready. If embedding is unavailable at query time, the system serves keyword-only results and says so. Indexing work waits in the queue with retries and a backoff.

failures.scenario: A mass edit, such as a wiki migration, adds 2 million events in an hour
failures.impact: The embedding workers fall far behind, and urgent edits and permission changes wait behind the bulk.
failures.answer: Events are put in separate queues by priority, so deletes and permission changes go first, then interactive edits, then bulk work. Bulk work is rate-limited and embedding capacity is scaled out. The freshness dashboard shows the backlog age, and the answer can warn that sources are still catching up.

failures.scenario: A new prompt makes answers worse on a topic nobody tested
failures.impact: Wrong answers go to thousands of people for days before anyone complains.
failures.answer: Releases go through the evaluation set and a canary share, and the online signals (thumbs down, follow-up rephrasing, answers with no citation) are watched per topic. A regression rolls back the prompt or model through a flag, and the failing questions are added to the evaluation set.

alternatives.title: How to apply permissions

options.name: Filter the candidates after retrieval
options.pro: Works with any index and is simple to build
options.con: Returns few or no results when the best matches are restricted, and wastes work

options.name: Filter inside the search, using ACL fields on each chunk
options.pro: Results are full and readable, and the ranking only sees allowed chunks
options.con: Needs a metadata copy that is kept in sync, and filters slow some vector indexes

options.name: A separate index per group or per user
options.pro: Strongest isolation and a fast query
options.con: Storage multiplies with the number of groups, and nested groups make it unmanageable

options.name: Ask the source system at query time
options.con: Slow, rate-limited, and some sources have no way to ask in bulk

alternatives.pick: Filter inside the search using synced ACL fields, plus a live check of the final few chunks.

alternatives.title: How to keep the index fresh

options.name: Nightly full crawl
options.con: A day of delay and a lot of wasted embedding work

options.name: Change events with content hashes
options.pro: Minutes of delay, and only changed chunks are embedded
options.con: Needs connectors per source and handling of missed events

options.name: Event-driven plus a periodic reconciliation
options.pro: Fast, and mistakes and missed deletes are repaired
options.con: Two code paths and extra read load on the sources

alternatives.pick: Events for speed, with a slow reconciliation sweep as the safety net.

alternatives.title: How to retrieve

options.name: Vector search only
options.pro: Finds paraphrases and works across languages
options.con: Misses exact identifiers and rare terms

options.name: Keyword search only
options.pro: Precise and cheap, with explainable matches
options.con: Fails when the question uses different words than the document

options.name: Hybrid with rank fusion, then a reranker
options.pro: Best recall and best precision of the three
options.con: More components, more latency, more settings to evaluate

alternatives.pick: Hybrid retrieval with rank fusion and a reranker on the top candidates.

alternatives.title: How to chunk

options.name: Fixed size with overlap
options.con: Cuts through sentences, lists and tables

options.name: By document structure (headings, paragraphs, table rows)
options.pro: Chunks keep their meaning and can carry a heading trail
options.con: Needs a parser per format and handling of messy documents

options.name: Small chunks for search, expanded to the parent section for the prompt
options.pro: Precise matching and enough context for the model
options.con: Two sizes to store and a lookup to expand them

alternatives.pick: Structure-aware chunks of a few hundred tokens, expanded to the section for the prompt when the budget allows.

roles.label: Sources and users
roles.description: Document systems and the employees who ask questions.

roles.label: Change queue
roles.description: Document events waiting to be indexed.

roles.label: Processing
roles.description: Parsing, embedding, retrieval, reranking and generation.

roles.label: State
roles.description: The chunk index, permissions, feedback and evaluation sets.

quiz.question: A nightly crawl re-embeds every document. At 10:00 someone edits the leave policy and deletes an outdated one, and at 11:00 the assistant still answers from both. The business wants edits searchable within 5 minutes and deletions gone within 1 minute. What is the right design?
options: Connectors emit change and delete events, the indexer re-embeds only changed chunks, and a periodic full listing catches missed events.
Run the same full crawl every hour on more embedding workers, which cuts the staleness from a day to under an hour for edits and deletions.
Show each answer's source last-modified date, so employees can judge for themselves whether a passage might be outdated or replaced by newer text.
Have the model open every cited source at answer time and refuse any passage that differs from the live document, leaving the index as it is.
quiz.explanation: Events make edits and deletions visible in minutes, and chunk hashes mean a one-word edit costs a few embeddings. An hourly crawl still misses both targets and wastes work re-embedding unchanged text. Showing a date only warns users, and a live check at answer time cannot find a newer document that was never retrieved.

quiz.question: An engineer asks about 'compensation bands'. The 50 best chunks by similarity all sit in an HR folder they cannot read, so the permission check applied after retrieval leaves nothing, although a readable page at rank 51 answers the question. What is the right fix?
options: Retrieve 500 candidates instead of 50 before the permission check, so enough readable chunks survive the filter every time.
Build one separate index per group and query only the indexes of the groups that the user belongs to at that moment.
Ask the source system whether the user can open each of the 50 candidates at query time and replace the rejected ones with the next best.
Store each document's access list on its chunks and filter by the user's group ids inside both the keyword and the vector search, then recheck the final chunks.
quiz.explanation: Filtering inside the search means the top results are all readable, so the ranking never wastes slots on restricted chunks. Fetching more candidates only moves the cliff, since a restricted topic can fill any number. Per-group indexes multiply storage with nested groups, and per-candidate source calls are slow and rate-limited.

quiz.question: A new embedding model scores 20% better on a public benchmark. A teammate proposes embedding only new and edited chunks with it from now on, leaving old chunks as they are, and embedding queries with the new model. What is the better plan?
options: Follow the proposal, because embeddings of the same text from any model land close together, so old and new vectors can share one index without any trouble at query time.
Build a second index with the new model for all chunks in the background, compare both on the team's evaluation questions, and switch queries over if it wins.
Overwrite the stored vectors in place with a nightly job that re-embeds chunks with the new model, so only one index has to be run.
Embed each query with both models and search the single mixed index, keeping the higher similarity score for every chunk.
quiz.explanation: Vectors from different models live in different spaces, so mixing them makes distances meaningless. A parallel index lets the team test on its own questions, switch at once, and roll back. An in-place overwrite leaves a half-converted index for days with no way back.
